s12.slug: FRIDAY · 11:40 PM · EL PASO, A GAS STATION OFF I-10 — THE TOWEL
body: The canopy lays the pumps out hard and white, six islands of it, and past the last island the lot gives out into gravel and then chain-link. Beyond the chain-link, below the grade of the interstate, runs a concrete channel with an international border down the middle of it, and beyond that a whole city has been spilled across the dark in orange and run up the side of a hill. Juárez. It looks like a lamp left on in a house the size of a county.

Margot brings the Odyssey in to pump four with the front tires exactly on the paint, sets the brake, and gets out of the driver’s seat in sections. She holds her right hand in her left and examines it. “I’d like it understood that I have not unclenched since Picacho,” she says. “I was passed outside Lordsburg by a horse trailer. The horse looked at me with what I can only describe as pity.”
Somebody has taped a square of cardboard across the card reader.
Kevin reads it aloud, as he has read aloud everything since Marisol: the speed limits, the mile markers, the warnings on the first-aid kit. “It’s twenty to twelve. I’ll go in. I have the clip.”
“Welcome to Texas, y’all,” Laney says from the side door, in a voice with the stuffing gone out of it. “Pay first and God bless.”
In Kevin’s quarter-zip the BlackBerry goes off with an alarm he must have set in California. The screen says CALL CLARE (TEXAS). Kevin looks at the clip, at the screen, at the clip.
“I’ll get it.”
Theo has not said a word in two hours, and the sentence has the sound of a hinge. He is already past the clip, with his own wallet out of his blazer.
“Four minutes,” Kevin tells the van, and heads down the lot toward the fence with the BlackBerry up, already smiling at it.

Through the store’s front glass Jack watches Theo put a question to the clerk that takes both hands. The clerk, reading glasses on a beaded chain and a SUN BOWL lanyard, answers, and Theo looks up into the ceiling tiles for the number as if it were stenciled there. He says one. It is a guess; you can tell from the parking lot. The clerk looks at the bill, at pump four through the window, at the Rolex, and rings it up. Over her head, on a bracket, a TV has the Capitol dome gone soft with snow and a reporter leaning into it in a parka, the sound off.

Theo comes back across the gravel with the slip, drops it in the way-back door pocket where the receipts go, hooks the nozzle’s latch the way Kevin showed him at Picacho, and leaves the pump to it. He goes off toward the ice machine with his hands in his blazer.

Jack takes the long way round to the restrooms, along the fence, because it leads away from the van. Kevin is at the chain-link with his back to Mexico, doing his Clare voice, which is his regular voice with the volume down and every consonant polished. “I know I said Texas. This is Texas. Respectfully, it counts.” And, a few steps on: “There’s a sign out on the interstate that says WATCH FOR WATER ON ROADWAY. In the desert. Clare, I think it’s a petition.” And: “Everyone’s fine. Everyone is hydrated. That’s the report.” And, softer, as Jack passes: “It’s good. Our Lady of La Vang has been over my head since California. She’s seen things.”

Behind him, at the corner of the building: “Okay. Okay, go to sleep. Call you from Louisiana.” When Jack looks back, Kevin is still at the fence with the call long over, his thumb pressing the red key as if the call might otherwise come back.

In the men’s room mirror, under the buzzing tube, a pink stripe runs down the side of Jack’s neck where the seat belt has been cutting in since Tucson. He holds his wrists under the cold tap and dries them on the Carhartt, the dispenser being empty.

Coming back along the front of the store he passes the ice machine, a white chest on legs with ICE across the lid in blue letters meant to look frosted. Theo has the lid propped on his shoulder and a drift of cold coming up over both of them. Laney stands in it in her beanie with a Styrofoam cup, her forehead almost on his lapel. Jack hears them from the corner before he has made out that they are talking.
“It was a mistake,” Theo says.
“The whole thing,” says Laney.
They see him. Theo first, then Laney, and two faces come up open for the next sentence, and there isn’t one. Behind them the machine drops its load into the bin, a long slide of it, and finishes.
“Yeah,” Jack says. He agrees with them.
“Costigan,” Theo says, and that is all there is. Jack nods to them both and goes on toward the van.

He is leaning on the side door when they come, a minute behind him and not together. Laney sits down on the sill with the pink train case from under her seat on her knees. She works the latch and takes out an orange bottle, tips one pill into her palm, and breaks it with her thumbnail, a small clean snap, and Theo’s hand comes down over her wrist.
“It’s a prescription, Theodore.”

He takes his hand back. She swallows one half with ice water out of the cup, puts the other half in the bottle, and presses the cap down and turns it until it clicks. Then she climbs into the van with the beanie already coming down over her eyes, and Theo is left in the open door with his hand held out a little from his side, where her wrist was.

At the far edge of the lot, past the last island, there is an air pump on a concrete pad, AIR 75¢, the hose coiled on top, and Jack walks out to it. The wind comes up off the channel with diesel in it and, under the diesel, something resinous that he would guess is the desert’s own and Margot could give a Latin name. Behind him a pump clicks off, and no one goes to the handle.
The tin is in the left pocket of the Carhartt. The Reds are in the right.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself.

choices.key: In El Paso, after the fight, you smoked one under the air pump.
response: The wind off the channel gets under the flame twice. He smokes it down to the letters with his back to the canopy, and the wind off the river takes it sideways toward Mexico.
Up on the interstate a truck downshifts for the exit and goes by. He takes his hand out of the right pocket empty, and stands there till it stops wanting anything.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Friday night in El Paso, by the air pump, after the van: eleven.

response: The bulb over the air pump has been dead for years, by the look of the hose. Under the air pump, where nobody is, he opens the tin and counts them with one finger. Eleven. He shuts it and puts it back where it lives.

response: Under the air pump he opens the tin a second time. Eleven. Still eleven. He shuts it.
